html:
The Late Period was the last age of native Egyptian kings, from 664 to 332 BCE, broken by two spells of Persian rule and ended by Alexander the Great. It began with the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling from the delta city of Sais.

Before it, Egypt had been ruled by kings from Nubia, the Twenty-fifth Dynasty from Kush, and then invaded by Assyria. Psamtik I began as an Assyrian vassal, but as Assyria weakened he made himself independent and reunited the country.

The Saite kings looked both back and outward:

  • Artists copied the styles of the Old Kingdom, two thousand years earlier, in a deliberate revival.
  • Kings hired Greek soldiers and let Greek merchants settle at Naukratis, opening Egypt to the Greek world.
  • Necho II began a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea.

In 525 BCE the Persian king Cambyses II conquered Egypt, and it became a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Around 450 BCE the Greek writer Herodotus travelled there and described it for his readers. The Egyptians revolted around 404 BCE and won back independence for about sixty years. Nectanebo II, who reigned until 343 BCE, was the last native Egyptian to rule Egypt for more than two thousand years.

Persia reconquered Egypt briefly. In 332 BCE Alexander the Great arrived and was welcomed as a liberator. After his death his general Ptolemy took Egypt, beginning Ptolemaic rule.
sum: The Late Period was the last age of native Egyptian kings, from 664 to 332 BCE, broken by two spells of Persian rule and ended by Alexander the Great. It began with the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling from the delta city of Sais.
